items.en: Your body needs time to find its balance again. Here’s what can help you better understand this stage, gently.

A miscarriage is the spontaneous end of a pregnancy, most often before the 12th to 14th week. It’s estimated that one in six to seven confirmed pregnancies ends this way, most often early in the pregnancy.

It isn’t rare, nor is it a sign of a future fertility problem. In the vast majority of cases, it’s linked to factors beyond anyone’s control, such as a chromosomal anomaly that occurred by chance during development.
A miscarriage isn’t caused by anything you did or didn’t do. You aren’t responsible for what happened.
Every experience is different from one person to another. Here are the most common signs:
Its intensity and duration can vary depending on the situation, then gradually decrease.
Pain similar to menstrual cramps, sometimes more intense, can accompany this stage.
Physical recovery usually spans a few days to a few weeks.
Your body generally takes a few weeks to regain hormonal balance after a miscarriage. A cycle can return as early as 4 to 6 weeks, but every journey is different.
Your body needs time to find its balance again, with no pressure to achieve a particular outcome.
Every journey is different: move at your own pace, without comparing yourself to others.
A medical check-up helps confirm that everything is progressing normally, with complete peace of mind. This appointment is also a chance to ask all your questions.
A conversation about what you’ve been through, an exam if needed, and space to answer your questions about what comes next.
If any of these signs appear, it’s important to contact a healthcare professional right away.
Signs that call for medical advice
Fever or a worsening general condition
Very heavy bleeding (needing to change your protection in less than an hour)
Taking care of your body doesn’t mean controlling everything: it mainly means giving yourself the time you need.

Missed pill: what to do? — AWA
A missed pill can happen to anyone. What to do mainly depends on how long ago you missed it, the type of pill, and when in the pack it happens.
Don’t panic. First check the exact type of your pill and check its package insert to find out the recommended course of action.
The package insert is your reference

For some pills, a delay of less than 12 hours generally doesn’t compromise contraceptive protection. In this case, the usual recommendation is to take the missed pill as soon as possible and then continue the pack at the usual time.
Take the pill as soon as you notice you’re late.
Then go back to your usual schedule for the following pills.
If you take the missed pill and then the one scheduled for the usual time, it can happen that two pills are taken on the same day.
When the delay exceeds the time allowed for your pill, protection may be reduced. What to do then depends on the type of pill, the number of pills missed, and where in the pack the missed pill falls.
Don’t rely only on the number of hours given here: some pills have different instructions. Always check your medication’s package insert.
The more quickly you react after noticing the missed pill, the easier it is to follow the appropriate recommendations.
The instructions can vary depending on the exact type of pill and the number of pills missed.
In some situations, a condom may be recommended for a given period.
Not all situations are alike. Some missed pills call for a more precise check of the recommendations.
What to do mainly depends on the time elapsed since the usual time of taking it.
This situation needs particular attention, and it’s best to check the package insert precisely.
A pharmacist or healthcare professional can quickly help you identify the right course of action.
Your pill’s package insert gives the precise instructions for the medication you’re taking. Recommendations can differ depending on whether it’s a combined pill or a progestin-only pill.
Keep the package insert handy (a photo on your phone, for example)
Contact a pharmacist if you have a quick question
See a doctor if it happens often
Why does the timing of the missed pill matter?
When the missed pill falls in the pack can change what to do. That’s why the package insert often gives different recommendations depending on the week of the pack.
If you don’t know what to do, it’s better to ask for advice than to stay in doubt. A pharmacist, midwife, or doctor can help you check the recommendations suited to your situation.

Frequent missed pills can be a sign that the daily routine doesn’t quite fit your lifestyle. Don’t hesitate to talk to a healthcare professional to explore other contraceptive options.
If taking a pill every day is hard to keep up, other methods exist with a different frequency of use.

Why your mood can vary throughout your cycle, though not always.
Mood across the phases of the cycle
Fluctuations in estrogen and progesterone directly influence mood-related neurotransmitters, such as serotonin.
Not every mood swing is necessarily linked to your cycle: life circumstances, stress, and fatigue also play an important role.
Fatigue and emotional sensitivity are common for many people.
This is often a phase of better energy and a greater sense of well-being.
Irritability or mood swings are more common during this time.
Premenstrual irritability or menopausal mood swings therefore have a real biological explanation, even if they don’t show up the same way for everyone.
Writing down your mood and your cycle phase helps you spot your own patterns.
Without judging yourself: the goal is to know yourself better, not to control everything.
Sleep, physical activity, and social support remain the best allies for stabilizing mood.
Lack of sleep often heightens emotional sensitivity.
Even moderate activity helps stabilize mood throughout the cycle.
Talking to someone you trust can ease what you’re feeling.
A mood change linked to your cycle is usually temporary. However, certain signs deserve particular attention:
Intense sadness, or sadness that persists beyond the cycle
A marked loss of interest in things you usually enjoy
A significant impact on your daily life or relationships
Intrusive thoughts or a significant feeling of distress
A doctor, midwife, or psychologist can help you better understand what you’re feeling and refer you to further support if needed.

What happens between fertilization and a positive pregnancy test.
After fertilization, the egg usually takes 6 to 10 days to reach the uterus and implant there: this is implantation. This step marks the true starting point of pregnancy.
Light bleeding or cramping can sometimes accompany implantation, though this isn’t systematic, nor a reliable sign on its own.
Mild cramping in the lower abdomen
No particular sign at all, for many women
The absence of a sign doesn’t mean anything: many pregnancies begin without any noticeable symptom at this stage.
It’s only after implantation that the hCG hormone starts being produced and becomes detectable by a pregnancy test. Testing too early can give a falsely negative result.
Waiting until the presumed day of your period before testing gives a more reliable result than testing too early.
Implantation happens discreetly, with or without a visible sign. A little patience before testing saves you from an unreliable result.
Understanding nifas, its duration, prayer, fasting, and the resumption of acts of worship after childbirth.
This content is purely educational. Religious questions should be validated by qualified scholars. AWA does not issue fatwas or personalized religious rulings.
Its duration according to jurisprudential references
Purification and resumption of acts of worship

In religious practice, nifas refers to the period linked to the bleeding after childbirth. Lochia describes the medical and physiological aspect of this bleeding; nifas is its religious classification. These two notions should not be confused.
AWA deliberately separates the medical information about lochia from the religious markers about nifas.
The maximum duration may vary according to the school of jurisprudence or the religious reference followed. 40 days is a frequently used reference, without being presented by AWA as a universal rule.
A frequently used reference is 40 days, but AWA does not present this figure as the one truth for all schools of jurisprudence. Follow the religious reference you have chosen.

During a period recognized as nifas according to the reference followed, ritual prayer is suspended. AWA does not automatically classify bleeding and does not provide a personalized decision. No missed-prayer counter is added for this period.
The obligatory fast is not performed during a period recognized as nifas. The days concerned are then handled through the appropriate make-up, according to the reference followed.
AWA can help you keep track of or organize the days concerned, without issuing a personalized religious decision.
Resumption depends on the signs observed and the religious reference followed.
Observe the end of the bleeding
Resume the acts of worship concerned
If the bleeding persists beyond the maximum duration adopted by the reference followed, its religious status may change. A qualified opinion is recommended.
No. 40 days is a frequently used reference, but jurisprudential references may differ.

The resumption of acts of worship depends on the signs observed and the religious reference followed.

If it exceeds the maximum duration adopted, its religious status may change: ask for a qualified opinion.

No. AWA provides general educational markers and does not issue a fatwa or a personalized decision.
Personal situations can differ. In case of doubt, reach out to a qualified scholar or a recognized religious organization.

After giving birth, the body goes through a gradual recovery period. Understanding postpartum bleeding, how it evolves, and the signs that call for attention can help you feel more informed during this time.
The term "Nifas" belongs to religious vocabulary and refers to the period associated with the bleeding that follows childbirth within the rules of Islamic jurisprudence.

Medically, the bleeding observed after childbirth is called "lochia." These two notions can be considered separately: one belongs to a religious framework, the other describes a physiological phenomenon.
A notion belonging to the religious framework after childbirth.
Medical term used for postpartum bleeding.
Postpartum recovery happens gradually. Postpartum bleeding generally changes over time as the uterus continues returning to its usual state.
The body gradually begins its recovery after birth.
The bleeding gradually changes in amount and color.
The bleeding generally decreases over time.
The menstrual cycle can then gradually resume.
Lochia generally changes color gradually and decreases in amount. However, this progression can vary from person to person.
The bleeding is usually red and can be heavier at the start.
The color can become lighter or brownish as the flow decreases.
The bleeding gradually becomes lighter and less abundant.
The color and amount of lochia can change gradually. The exact progression isn’t the same for everyone.

The key moment of your cycle, and how to recognize it.
The signs that may come with it
Ovulation is the release of an egg by one of the ovaries. It usually occurs about 14 days before your next period, regardless of your cycle’s total length.
It’s the date of your next period that varies from woman to woman, much more than the time between ovulation and its arrival.
Certain physical signs may accompany the approach of ovulation, to varying degrees depending on the woman.
As ovulation approaches, cervical mucus becomes clearer, stretchier, and more elastic.
Mild pain on one side of the lower abdomen ("mittelschmerz")
A slight rise in basal body temperature after ovulation
A boost of energy in some women
Observing these signs over several cycles helps you get to know your own rhythm, which can differ from general averages.
A cycle without ovulation can occasionally happen, without this necessarily being a cause for concern. If your period is absent for a long time or you’re unsure, medical advice is recommended.
No single sign is perfectly reliable on its own: combining them gives a better idea of your most fertile time.
A weekly alternative to the daily pill.
The patch continuously releases hormones through the skin, working in a way comparable to the combined pill: it prevents ovulation and thickens cervical mucus.
Its main advantage is that it doesn’t require a daily dose.
The patch is generally changed once a week for three weeks, followed by one week without a patch.
